title: What closed testers taught me about the interface of my AI-assisted Godot RTS, Estandarte
author: SouthernReach143
selftext:
I'm Diego, developing Estandarte, a medieval RTS for Android, in Godot with substantial AI coding assistance. I shared the resource-delivery side of the project here earlier. I'm now preparing its Google Play pre-registration phase.



The most useful recent feedback has been about things a new player has to understand immediately. One tester described choppy graphics and animations, buildings that were difficult to identify, and text that needed to be easier to read. That gives me concrete priorities when iterating with AI: which building the player recognizes, what the first confusing action is, and whether movement is readable on an actual phone. I still need to verify the next changes with players.



In the game, villagers physically deliver resources to depots before they become spendable. Players place the village buildings and directly command workers and troops. Showing that delivery rule clearly on a small screen has become as much an interface task as a simulation task. English and Spanish text are available.



For other people building simulation games with AI assistance, how do you turn a vague report such as 'this feels choppy' into a useful next iteration? Do you ask for a short recording of one action, device details, or a repeatable test scene first?



Official listing: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.estandarte.valle](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.estandarte.valle)

Pre-registration activation is pending Google's review. Once enabled, signing up for the launch notification will be free; the game will be paid at launch, and pre-registration does not give immediate access to play.

comments.author: DamnrightWorldsDev
comments.body: I always copy&paste the feedback to my agent(s) and ask "how should we handle this feedback?" and based on that, I'll just keep iterating until it's perfect.
